Triggers.value: People who look similar to the victims
When people say things like my ex

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

vignette:
Priya is a 37-year-old South Asian woman who has been married for nine years and runs a small gift and stationery shop in a mid-sized American city. She presented for psychological assessment reporting a PCL-5 score of 72, describing a level of distress that had, in her own words, begun to make her feel like a stranger inside her own life.

Approximately fourteen months before seeking help, Priya was sexually assaulted by a man she had been acquainted with through a former social circle - someone her husband had never met, someone she had trusted enough to meet briefly in a public setting before he coerced her into an isolated space. The assault was prolonged. What stayed with her most viscerally was not only what he did, but the particular quality of his voice - the way he used her name, the way he spoke about their shared connections as though they were a form of intimacy - and the fact that she had frozen entirely, had said nothing, had in some part of herself tried to make the situation feel manageable by going still and accommodating. She had not screamed. She had not fought. In the weeks that followed, this became the fact around which her inner life organised itself most painfully.

In the immediate aftermath, Priya told no one. She returned to the shop the next morning, opened the register, and greeted customers. But something had shifted in the architecture of how she moved through the world. She found she could not reconstruct what had happened in any ordered, verbal way - when she tried to think through it, the experience surfaced not as a narrative but as sensation, as smell, as the particular angle of afternoon light through a window. She could not put it into words, and this frightened her, as though the absence of language meant the event had colonised something deeper than memory.

Certain things became unbearable without her fully understanding why at first. A customer coming into the shop who shared a physical resemblance to her assailant - similar height, similar build, a particular way of carrying himself - would cause her to feel, for a terrible few seconds, that she was back in that room. These moments arrived without warning and left her gripping the edge of the counter, certain the threat was present and immediate. She repositioned the shop's small service desk so that her back was always against the rear wall and she could see the full length of the store. She told her husband it was better for customer flow. When she remembered the assault - and she remembered it often - the terror she had felt in the room returned with the same force as if it were happening again, accompanied almost immediately by a crushing sense of guilt, a certainty that her stillness, her compliance, had been a choice rather than a response, that she had failed herself in some fundamental way.

She stopped taking the city bus, which she had used for years to commute to a weekend market where she sourced inventory. She told herself the routes had changed, then simply stopped going to the market. A supplier relationship she had maintained for six years quietly dissolved. Her husband noticed the shop's stock had grown thin but accepted her explanations. Around people who felt unpredictable - a raised voice, someone gesturing quickly near her - she became accommodating to the point of self-erasure, agreeing to things she did not want, smoothing over tensions before they could form, as though keeping the temperature of every room low was the only reliable form of safety available to her. Hearing a customer mention an ex-partner in passing, or catching a name that rhymed with or resembled her assailant's, could collapse the distance between the present moment and that afternoon in ways she could not predict or control.

What finally brought Priya to seek help was a conversation with her husband in which he gently said he felt he had lost her. She had no words to dispute it. She arrived at her first session quiet and watchful, seated with her back against the wall of the waiting room. What she feared most was that putting the event into language - if she could even manage it - would confirm what she already suspected about herself. What she hoped for, almost too quietly to say aloud, was that she might one day stop feeling like the person who had gone still.
